name: Portfolio Allocation Analysis
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Building the Actual Portfolio: From Correlation to Position Size
lesson.summary: Portfolio allocation takes the correlation logic from diversification and the engineering-versus-deep-uncertainty split from the required breakthroughs and turns both into an actual number, how much of a portfolio each kind of bet deserves.
lesson.body:
Portfolio diversification told you that owning several quantum labeled stocks is not automatically diversified, because correlation, not variety, is what actually spreads risk. Each breakthrough is uncertain told you that the seven required breakthroughs are not equally uncertain, some are engineering problems likely to yield to sustained investment, others depend on scientific discoveries that may or may not exist to be found. Portfolio allocation analysis is what happens when you stop treating those as two separate lessons and use them together to answer a concrete question: given a fixed amount of money, how much actually goes where.

Start with a hypothetical investor allocating a 100,000 dollar frontier technology sleeve of a larger portfolio, purely as an illustration. A first pass might identify four candidate exposures: a fault-tolerant quantum computing company betting on superconducting qubits, a second fault-tolerant company betting on trapped ions, a quantum sensing company selling gravimeters today, and a classical AI hardware company. Simply splitting evenly across all four, 25,000 dollars each, looks diversified on a spreadsheet and is not, because the two fault-tolerant bets share the same underlying deep uncertainty, whether error corrected computing at meaningful scale arrives at all, even though they differ in hardware architecture. A setback in the field's confidence about that timeline moves both of them together.

The correction is to size positions by what actually has to go right, not by how many tickers there are. The quantum sensing company's success depends mostly on manufacturing execution and market adoption, engineering and business uncertainty with a track record of yielding to sustained effort. The classical AI hardware company depends on demand growth continuing at an already proven, already revenue generating pace. Both belong closer to the engineering end of the uncertainty spectrum and can reasonably support a larger combined position, say 60,000 dollars split between them, sized in proportion to how resolved their core technical questions already are. The two fault-tolerant computing bets, by contrast, both depend on breakthroughs sitting on the deep uncertainty end, including the new algorithms question that no amount of funding guarantees gets solved on schedule. A disciplined allocation caps their combined size well below an even split, say 40,000 dollars total split unevenly with the stronger team getting more, sized as a genuine venture style bet rather than a core holding, precisely because their outcomes are correlated with each other and with a scientific question that might not resolve on any predictable timeline.

This is the same discipline a venture fund applies when it distinguishes a core position from a moonshot, just made explicit and defensible instead of intuitive. The size of a position should track two things simultaneously: how correlated it is with the portfolio's other holdings, and how much of its success depends on deep uncertainty rather than engineering uncertainty. A company whose success requires several unresolved deep uncertainty breakthroughs to land together earns a smaller position than one whose success requires only continued execution on already understood physics, even if the first company's story is more exciting to tell at dinner.

None of this produces a single correct allocation, reasonable investors with different time horizons and different risk tolerance will land on different numbers, and that is expected rather than a flaw in the method. What the method guarantees is that the allocation was built from an honest accounting of correlation and uncertainty type rather than from how many different logos happened to have the word quantum on them. That same logic, applied not to one investor's sleeve but to an entire nation's research budget, is exactly the lens the next chapter turns on government quantum strategy.
